title: Zombie Process Accumulation
exclusions: Detects repeated Linux `ps` snapshots containing processes whose state begins with `Z`. It does not identify the parent process because the supported `Splunk_TA_nix` `ps.sh` fields do not include `PPID`, prove why the parent failed to reap its child, inspect a container's PID namespace independently of the host, detect processes between collection polls, or establish service impact or regulatory compliance. The primary SPL applies no maintenance exclusion.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_zombie_process_accumulation_15m` saved-search definition, scheduler and alert history, and result exports containing `first_bucket`, `last_bucket`, `host`, `zombie_threshold`, `observed_buckets`, `breach_buckets`, `min_zombie_count`, `max_zombie_count`, `current_zombie_count`, and `zombie_processes`. These artifacts show that indexed snapshots met the rule; they do not prove collection completeness or root cause.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with the `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge, index three complete `sourcetype=ps` table snapshots for `host=zombie-test-positive` in three adjacent closed five-minute buckets. Each snapshot must contain at least one valid non-zombie row and exactly five distinct numeric `PID` rows whose `STAT` (or legacy `S`) value starts with `Z`. Run the SPL with fixed bounds over those buckets. Expect one row with `observed_buckets=3`, `breach_buckets=3`, and all three zombie-count fields equal to 5.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Index three equivalent snapshots for `host=zombie-test-negative`, but include only four zombie PIDs in the middle bucket; use `S`, `R`, or another non-`Z` state for the remaining process row. Run the same fixed-bounds search. Expect zero rows because only two of the three buckets meet `zombie_threshold=5`. Also verify that a command containing the text `<defunct>` with state `S` does not count as a zombie.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=ps` multi-line process snapshots produced by the `ps.sh` scripted event input in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). The SPL uses `multikv` to create one search result per table row. Current Linux output uses `PID`, `STAT`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; add-on 8.7.0+ documentation maps legacy `S` to raw `STAT` and preserves backward compatibility. `_time` and `host` are Splunk metadata. The index name is a deployment choice.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), installed on Linux collection forwarders and on the Splunk tier that supplies its parsing and search-time knowledge.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os sourcetype=ps host=* earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| multikv
| eval process_id=tostring(coalesce(PID,pid,process_id)), process_state=trim(coalesce(STAT,S,stat)), process_name=coalesce(COMMAND,process_name,"(command unavailable)"), process_user=coalesce(USER,user,"(user unavailable)")
| where match(process_id,"^[0-9]+$") AND isnotnull(process_state)
| eval is_zombie=if(match(process_state,"^Z"),1,0), zombie_pid=if(is_zombie=1,process_id,null()), zombie_detail=if(is_zombie=1,process_name." [PID=".process_id.", USER=".process_user.", STATE=".process_state."]",null())
| stats dc(zombie_pid) as zombie_count values(zombie_detail) as zombie_processes count as parsed_process_rows by _time host
| eval observed_at=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| stats latest(zombie_count) as zombie_count latest(zombie_processes) as zombie_processes latest(parsed_process_rows) as parsed_process_rows latest(observed_at) as observed_at by _time host
| eval zombie_threshold=5, breached=if(zombie_count>=zombie_threshold,1,0)
| stats count as observed_buckets sum(breached) as breach_buckets min(zombie_count) as min_zombie_count max(zombie_count) as max_zombie_count latest(zombie_count) as current_zombie_count latest(zombie_processes) as zombie_processes min(_time) as first_bucket max(_time) as last_bucket by host zombie_threshold
| where observed_buckets=3 AND breach_buckets=3
| convert ctime(first_bucket) ctime(last_bucket)
| sort 0 -current_zombie_count host
description: Reports one row per Linux host when the latest process snapshot in each of three consecutive closed five-minute buckets contains at least five distinct processes in zombie state. It expands the add-on's table event into process rows, recognizes both current `STAT` and legacy `S` fields, and counts numeric process identifiers rather than counting snapshot events.
value: Detecting persistent unreaped children helps operators correct faulty parent-process lifecycle handling before zombie growth consumes process identifiers and prevents new work from starting. Requiring the condition in three complete buckets reduces noise from normal exit/reap timing while preserving process names and identifiers for triage.
implementation: Deploy Splunkbase 833 and enable the supplied `ps.sh` scripted event input on Linux hosts; use a five-minute collection interval unless a measured need justifies higher-volume polling. Verify that `multikv` yields numeric `PID`, current `STAT` or legacy `S`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`. Save the search to run every five minutes on bucket boundaries. Its initial threshold is five zombies in each of three buckets, a tunable operational policy rather than a Linux or Splunk limit.
visualization: Use a latest-alert table with `host`, `current_zombie_count`, `min_zombie_count`, `max_zombie_count`, `zombie_threshold`, and `zombie_processes`. Add a 24-hour line chart of per-snapshot zombie count by host with the configured threshold overlaid, plus a collection-completeness panel for `sourcetype=ps`. Do not chart the number of raw snapshot events as the number of zombies.
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on's source-type table classifies `sourcetype=ps` under Performance, but CIM Performance 6.4 has no process-state or zombie-process dataset. No equivalent accelerated `tstats` search is claimed; the rule must expand the source table and use the add-on-specific `STAT`/`S` and `PID` fields.

knownFalsePositives:
A `Z` state is not a fabricated match: Linux defines it as a terminated process that has not been reaped. The alert can nevertheless be operationally expected or misleading in these circumstances:

1. **Short parent/child scheduling delay** — A child can be visible as a zombie briefly before its parent calls a wait function. The three-bucket rule is designed to exclude this; do not lower persistence without measuring normal process-exit behavior.

2. **Approved application or supervisor test** — A fault-injection or lifecycle test can deliberately leave children unreaped. Confirm the exact host, service owner, test identifier, and bounded change window before suppressing the alert.

3. **Container PID-namespace mismatch** — Host `ps` can show a process identifier and command that differ from the container operator's view. Resolve the host PID to its namespace and workload before declaring the alert stale; the detection is host-scoped, not pod-scoped.

4. **Duplicate or malformed table extraction** — Replayed snapshots, a missing header, or a locally modified `ps.sh` format can produce misleading rows. The SPL counts distinct numeric PIDs per snapshot and requires three buckets, but operators must still compare `parsed_process_rows` and raw tables with the host.

5. **PID reuse across different snapshots** — PID reuse does not inflate a single snapshot's distinct count, but the same number can refer to a different process later. Treat `zombie_processes` as latest-snapshot triage context, not durable process identity.

**Safe suppression:** if policy requires exceptions, add a separate owner-approved lookup keyed by exact `host` and, where stable, `process_name`, with start and end epochs, reason, ticket, and approver. Apply it after computing the base result, retain suppressed matches for review, and reject wildcard or non-expiring exclusions.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal boundary

Install a release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) that the current compatibility table supports for the deployed Splunk platform and Linux versions. Put the collection configuration on each Universal Forwarder that will execute `ps.sh`, and make the add-on's parsing and search-time knowledge available on the tiers required by the deployment topology. The Splunkbase listing warns that version 6.0 changed default indexes and configuration files, so test upgrades outside production. Follow Splunk's documented execution-permission and operating-system privilege requirements. Grant the operations search role access to the selected operating-system index and permission to schedule this search, without granting unrelated index access.

Linux documents `Z` as a zombie: a process that terminated but has not been reaped by its parent. It no longer executes, but it retains a process-table entry until the parent obtains its status with a wait operation or exits and the child is adopted and reaped. A handful of momentary zombies is not equivalent to resource exhaustion. This rule therefore detects five or more distinct zombie PIDs in three consecutive complete buckets. Five and fifteen minutes are catalogue starting points, not kernel, procps, or Splunk vendor limits; baseline each workload class before changing them.

The add-on's supported `ps.sh` collector does not document `PPID` as an output field. Do not add a fictitious `PPID` dependency to the SPL. The alert identifies the affected host, PID, user, command, and state; parent identification is an on-host response step.

## 1. Enable and verify the supplied `ps.sh` input

Use the stanza already shipped in the installed add-on. Copy only that stanza from `Splunk_TA_nix/default/inputs.conf` to `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`; Splunk explicitly advises against copying the entire default file because local copies persist across upgrades. Preserve the installed script path and source-type settings, set the local event index, and choose a measured interval. A five-minute example is:

```ini
[script://./bin/ps.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 300
index = os
```

`interval=300` is this use case's collection design, not a claimed add-on default. A shorter interval indexes a complete process table more often and can materially increase ingest volume. If the deployment uses an index other than `os`, change the stanza and SPL together. Restart or deploy the forwarder configuration according to the normal change procedure, then inspect the effective stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` to confirm the local override wins.

Search `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m` and inspect `_raw`. A snapshot must retain its header and process rows because `multikv` derives field names from the header and creates one search event per row. Test with `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m | multikv | table _time host PID STAT S COMMAND USER`. On current Linux output, expect numeric `PID`, raw `STAT`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; older add-on output used `S`. Splunk's add-on documentation says the 8.7.0 redesign maps old `S` to raw `STAT` while preserving old fields, so the SPL coalesces both names. `STAT` can contain characters after the primary state, and the Linux `ps` manual defines a leading `Z` as zombie, hence `match(process_state,"^Z")` rather than a search for `<defunct>` text.

Compare one snapshot on the same host with `ps -eo user:32,pid,ppid,stat,comm,args --sort=pid`. Allow for the collection and forwarding delay. Confirm every host-side `Z` row appears after `multikv`, and spot-check healthy `S` and `R` rows. The on-host `PPID` is intentionally available for triage even though it is not part of this search's required add-on fields. Record any command truncation: the add-on documents a command-length limit, so `COMMAND` is context and must not be treated as a globally unique process identity.

## 2. Save and understand the accumulation search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_zombie_process_accumulation_15m` and schedule it every five minutes on five-minute boundaries. Its explicit `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m` window selects three closed buckets while leaving five minutes for the newest snapshot to arrive. This adds detection latency deliberately; deployments with proven lower forwarding delay can redesign the bounds, but must rerun the positive and negative controls.

`multikv` expands each multi-line table snapshot. The first `eval` coalesces current and legacy field names; the numeric-PID filter discards the header or malformed rows. `is_zombie` tests the leading process-state character. `dc(zombie_pid)` counts distinct zombie PIDs in each original snapshot, while `parsed_process_rows` provides a data-quality clue. The second aggregation bins snapshots and keeps the latest snapshot in each five-minute bucket, avoiding inflation if the input happens to run more than once per bucket.

The rule sets `zombie_threshold=5`, marks each bucket independently, and then requires exactly three observed buckets and three breached buckets. A host with a missing bucket or one bucket below five produces no alert. Trigger the saved alert when result count is greater than zero. Include all returned fields, notify once per host, and use incident-system deduplication by host rather than a long Splunk throttle that hides continued accumulation. If a host class normally carries persistent zombies, fix or formally accept the parent-process behavior before increasing the threshold; do not tune solely to make pages disappear.

The add-on labels `ps` as Performance data, but CIM Performance 6.4 does not provide process-state or zombie-count fields. Do not substitute CPU load, memory use, or an Endpoint process-start data set and call it equivalent. No `cimSpl` is provided because a `tstats` search would change the detection's meaning.

## 3. Validate data and rule behavior

Create test snapshots that reproduce the add-on's actual aligned header and rows; do not test only pre-made scalar fields, because table extraction is part of this control. Place the positive fixture described in `controlTest` in three adjacent closed buckets. Each snapshot needs five distinct numeric zombie PIDs and at least one healthy row. Run a copy of the SPL with the temporary index and fixed earliest/latest times. Confirm one result, three observed and breached buckets, and counts of five. Drill into `zombie_processes` and verify that it lists only the five `Z` rows from the latest bucket.

For the negative fixture, change the middle snapshot to four zombies. Expect no final result. Inspect the pipeline immediately before the final `where` and confirm `observed_buckets=3` and `breach_buckets=2`; this distinguishes correct threshold rejection from a collection failure. Also test three failure cases: omit one snapshot and expect `observed_buckets=2`; use a nonnumeric PID and confirm that row is discarded; put `<defunct>` in a command with state `S` and confirm it is not counted.

On a staging host, compare at least two successive indexed snapshots with the on-host `ps` command. Use `timechart span=5m count by host` over the raw source type to find silent collection periods, and separately track `parsed_process_rows` for abrupt extraction changes. These are documentation and synthetic-search procedures until actually executed. This editorial review did not index fixtures, run a Splunk search, or validate a production add-on/platform combination.

## 4. Operationalize, investigate, and preserve evidence

Build a latest-results table and a 24-hour count trend. A separate collection-health panel should show last event time and raw snapshot count per host; a quiet zombie panel must never be presented as proof that collection is healthy. Restrict raw process arguments to appropriate operators because command lines can expose paths, tenant names, or secrets supplied unsafely by applications.

When the alert fires, connect through the approved administration path and run `ps -eo user:32,pid,ppid,stat,lstart,comm,args --sort=ppid,pid`. Confirm that the reported PIDs still exist and retain a leading `Z`. Group them by PPID, then inspect the parent with `ps -p <ppid> -o pid,ppid,user,stat,lstart,comm,args`. Review service-manager status, application logs, recent deployments, and container namespace ownership. A zombie cannot be repaired by sending it `SIGKILL`; it has already terminated. Correct action is normally for the parent to reap children, or for an owner-approved restart/upgrade of the faulty parent. Never have the alert automatically kill a parent, restart a service, or reboot a host.

Retain the saved-search export, scheduler history, result rows, and relevant raw snapshot according to the operations-log policy. Capture the parent PID and application incident in the response record if identified. These artifacts show configured monitoring and a matched state; they do not demonstrate that every process was observed or that a regulatory obligation was satisfied.

## 5. Troubleshoot and suppress safely

No `ps` events usually means the supplied input remains disabled, the add-on is absent from the forwarder, the script or its directory lacks required execution permission, routing targets another index, or the search role cannot read the index. Raw snapshots without row fields usually indicate that the search-tier knowledge is missing, the sourcetype changed, the header was removed, or an ingest transformation damaged the complete event. Use `btool`, the forwarder's `splunkd.log`, and the add-on's documented debug workflow to identify the failing layer.

If `S` is present but `STAT` is absent, the host or add-on is using the legacy format; the SPL supports it. If neither exists, do not search `COMMAND` for `<defunct>` as a silent workaround—repair extraction and revalidate. If zombie counts exceed an on-host check, compare snapshot time, PID namespace, duplicate collection stanzas, and the raw table. If they are lower, inspect event truncation, command visibility, and header/row completeness.

The primary SPL has no hidden allow-list. For an approved test, implement a separate exact-host, time-bounded exception lookup with owner, reason, ticket, and expiry, and preserve the base match before suppression. Avoid command-substring or fleet-wide exclusions: command text can be truncated or reused, and a broad exception can hide a different faulty parent. Review every exception at expiry and remove it when the test or accepted defect ends.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for a growing group of finished programs that a Linux server has not cleaned up properly. If they remain for several checks, the team can fix the program responsible before the server has trouble starting new work.
